author: Moksh Trehan
capture_note: All photographs in this report were supplied by the author for this assignment. Three overlapping sets depict a basketball court, an indoor lounge, and a city view; two additional photographs show book covers for rectification. The intended mosaic model is camera rotation about a fixed center. Camera motion was not measured, and depth-dependent residuals are consistent with foreground parallax and departures from that model.

scene1.capture: Three central frames of the basketball-court sweep (IMG_1242–1244) share the window wall and backboard. IMG_1243 is the reference.
scene1.manual: Twelve manually observed window-frame landmarks constrain each adjacent pair. The displayed mosaic uses two-band blending and preserves the hoop from the reference photograph. The original feather-only result is retained below for comparison.
scene1.comparison: Both displayed results use the same two-band compositor and the same manually specified reference-source region around the hoop. The backboard, rim, and net therefore remain intact in both. Their sharpness is a compositing result and does not establish better homography accuracy; differences in the unprotected lower-window crop show the remaining geometric disagreements.
scene1.limitations: The backboard, net, window structure, and distant exterior lie at different depths. A single homography cannot align all of them if the camera translates. Source selection removes duplicated hoop edges locally; it does not correct parallax elsewhere, and ownership transitions can still leave seams.
scene1.refinement_caption: Automatic geometric estimate, identical before and after source selection. Left: feathering averages displaced edges. Right: the whole hoop, backboard, and net come from IMG_1243; no content is synthesized.
refinement_note: The initial feathered mosaic doubled the backboard and rim because the foreground object occupies slightly different locations across the views. A source-selection refinement keeps this object intact while retaining the estimated homographies.

In the 1400-pixel-wide IMG_1243 reference frame, the manually specified rectangle x = 340–900, y = 140–560 uses that photograph exclusively across all frequency bands. A 72-pixel cosine transition lies outside the rectangle. Elsewhere, the two-band compositor retains sharper detail. The same physical region is applied to both manual and automatic geometry.

Protected pixels exactly equal the registered reference image before export, and the source-coverage mask is unchanged. This is a documented compositing intervention after geometric estimation; the automatic feather baseline remains visible below.
scene1.detail_caption: Manual (left) and automatic (right): the lower window and net outside the protected hoop rectangle, cropped at identical reference coordinates.

scene2.capture: Four overlapping lounge views, ordered IMG_1247, IMG_1248, IMG_1250, IMG_1249. IMG_1248 is the reference; the last two images are ordered by scene overlap rather than filename.
scene2.manual: Manual points emphasize static door frames, artwork, the fireplace, and stone-wall details. The room is recognizable across all four views, with local doubling around the furniture and ceiling fixture.
scene2.comparison: The automatic result has sharper stone courses and a more consistent artwork frame in the common-coordinate detail. The manual result shows more widespread softness across the wall. Both retain displaced edges around objects nearer to the camera.
scene2.limitations: Foreground furniture, the chandelier, and the corridor are not coplanar with the fireplace wall. Differences in viewpoint and exposure leave ghosting and broad intensity transitions that feathering cannot fully correct.

scene3.capture: Three overlapping outdoor views (IMG_1251–1253), with IMG_1252 as the reference. Buildings provide static landmarks distributed across the lower half of the images; the sky is not used for manual annotations.
scene3.manual: Ten and eleven visually selected landmarks constrain the two adjacent pairs. Refining ambiguous roof tips and using clear roof corners reduced the fitting residuals; the rooflines and chimney now remain sharp across most overlaps.
scene3.comparison: Both methods recover a coherent panorama from the same three photographs. The manual fits use 10 and 11 carefully observed landmarks, while the automatic fits retain 137/153 and 108/127 descriptor matches. These are fitting statistics, not independent accuracy measurements.
scene3.limitations: Most landmarks are below the horizon, so the upper sky and outer image boundaries are extrapolated. Thin roof edges remain sensitive to small point-placement errors; the clouds are not assumed to be fixed geometric landmarks.

descriptor_caption: One actual matched feature from each reference image. Left: the original 40 × 40 grayscale neighborhood. Middle: the same neighborhood after Gaussian blur (σ = 2). Right: eight samples per axis, five pixels apart, normalized to zero mean and unit standard deviation. Normalized displays share the range −2 to +2; the exact 64 values are saved with the figure data.

validation.summary: Checks cover homography recovery and degenerate inputs, explicit inverse sampling and valid black pixels, ANMS and descriptors, ratio matching, RANSAC with outliers, transform chains, and project configuration. An independent degeneracy audit re-fitted all seven automatic photograph pairs from their saved matches; the corrected validation produced identical matrices, inlier masks, and trial counts. Five additional tests verify mask handling, detail ownership, and constant-field preservation in the optional two-band compositor. Two further tests verify that protected reference pixels remain exact and that the transition preserves coverage.

blend_caption: Optional two-band extension on the lounge, using identical automatic homographies and coverage. Detail ownership reduces duplicated chandelier edges and clarifies masonry while broad feathering softens exposure changes. Remaining overlap seams show that blending cannot repair parallax.
